newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Tel Aviv bomber not in the mould.
newsitem.headline: Tel Aviv bomber not in the mould.

text.p: Musa Ghneimat, a father of four, walked nervously into a Tel Aviv cafe, sat at a table, and detonated a bag of explosives, killing a mother, an expectant mother and another woman.
What drove a family man to ruin the lives of other families relaxing over a drink in the spring sunshine last Friday?
The promise of eternal life dangled before a weak and impressionable character, say psychologists who have studied Palestinian suicide attackers.
Ghneimat, 28, was from the village of Sourif, near Hebron, the West Bank stronghold of the Islamic fundamentalist group Hamas.
But he did not fit the profile of the suicide bombers that have struck Israel since the Hebron massacre three years ago.
He had a wife, two sons and two daughters. He was older than the others. He had a job. He didn't live in a refugee camp.

"He was an educated guy...of European appearance," said a manager of the Formaggio restaurant near Tel Aviv, where Ghneimat worked illegally. "I remember we would sit until the early hours of the morning and exchange experiences," said the manager who did not give his name.

Ghneimat's Arab acquaintances remember him as man with only a basic education who went regularly to the mosque. He was detained by Israel for 18 days in 1988 on suspicion of aiding Hamas, residents of his village said.
One of his six brothers was arrested for aiding Qassam, the military wing of Hamas, they said.
But Ghneimat kept a low profile in Israel where he worked for the past 10 years, mostly illegally, washing dishes and cleaning. He spoke Hebrew but never talked politics, co-workers recalled.
"He does not fit the average profile," said Iyad Sarraj a Palestinian psychiatrist who has studied suicide killers.
"But the basic drive for self-destruction is the same...They all believe that they are not going to die, that they are moving from one phase of life to a higher one," Sarraj said.
Many Moslem scholars dispute the interpretation that those who indiscriminately kill women and children become martyrs, who go to a reward in paradise where rivers of honey and 72 virgins await them.
But the vision of such an afterlife can be a powerful draw to those who have weak minds or vengeful hearts.
The accounts of those who have escaped the clutches of their Hamas handlers shine some light into this dark side of the human psyche.
Musa Ziada tried out a grave as part of his training. He was being groomed to overcome the fear of death but he never got to paradise.

Ziada's uncle, a member of the Palestinian security service, noticed that the then 15-year-old was spending a lot of time at the mosque in the Gaza Strip's Bureij refugee camp with a known member of Hamas.
His suspicions saved his nephew's life. Ziada's story surfaced in 1995.

"In the beginning they were teaching me pure religious lessons," Ziada said at a news conference in 1995. "Then they talked a lot about martyrdom and frightend me with stories of hell. They advised me to move on the path to paradise...they took me to the cemetery and told me to lie in the grave."
Hamas officials dismissed Ziada's account but it accords with testimony by other would-be bombers and the relatives of successful bombers.
Teachers take their pupils through three major stages. First religious indoctrination, then the linking of current politics to that religious knowledge, and finally, action.

Japanese kamikaze pilots and Tamil suicide bombers show that murderous self-sacrifice is not limited to Arabs. But Sarraj believes the idea of dying for one's community is deeply rooted in the Middle East.

Bombers are told that when the very first drop of their blood is spilled it cleanses all their sins and sends them to paradise where 72 virgins await their pleasure. Seventy of their relatives will also receive absolution and a place in paradise. The bomber will be crowned with glory and achieve the ultimate -- see the face of Allah.
On earth, Hamas will give them a martyr's funeral and look after their loved ones.
Another insight into motive comes in an affidavit to a human rights group by the very first bomber, Ra'ed Zakarna, who killed eight people in the northern Israeli town of Afula on April 13, 1994.

In two and a half pages of testimony he details how he was beaten, hooded and threatened with rape by a male interrogator during 12 weeks of relentless questioniong in an Israeli jail in 1993. He was freed without charge. The next year he went to Afula.
"Suicide bombings are not prohibited for these Islamists because they consider it holy war against Jews, and every Jew is an enemy and every Israeli is a potential soldier," Sarraj said.
Bombers are taught that the conquest by Jews of the Moslem land of Palestine can be overturned only by the sword of Islam.
